paragraphs.text: A brick of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, the branch of pu’er that is never darkened by fast fermentation. Like all raw pu’er it begins as large-leaf tea that is [fried in a wok to kill the green](sheng:making), rolled and dried in the sun rather than by hot air, so some of the leaf’s own activity survives and lets the tea keep changing for years.

Tea was first [pressed](sheng:pressing) so it could travel, packed compact onto pack animals along the old trade routes, and the pressing still decides how it ages: a tight, large piece changes slowly, a loose or small one faster. With no rapid fermentation behind it, this brick [changes through storage](sheng:aging), so where it has been kept is part of its history, not a promise of quality.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: In young raw pu’er, a bitter, drying bite that turns into a returning sweetness, a feel in the throat that makes the mouth water, and fresh, floral or fruity notes such as apricot or plum. Tea kept in humid storage can carry a damp, earthy storage taste.
